items.title: Star performers always come back down — not because of psychology
items.claim: A rookie has a breakout season. The next year, his performance drops. Headlines say 'sophomore slump' and 'pressure of expectations'. A statistician would have predicted the drop without ever watching a game.

options.text: Extreme observations have a luck component; the next observation typically regresses toward the underlying mean. The 'rookie season' was partially luck; the next season's mean performance reflects underlying skill, with less luck

items.reveal_title: Galton, sons of tall fathers, and luck
items.reveal:
Francis Galton (1886) measured heights of fathers and sons. He noticed: tall fathers tend to have shorter sons, and short fathers tend to have taller sons. Not because fathers' height 'reverts' to a population mean, but because extreme parental heights are partly random (chance of which alleles were inherited from grandparents).

Galton called this 'regression to mediocrity', later 'regression to the mean'. The term 'regression analysis' for fitting lines to data descends from this observation.

General principle: if a measurement combines skill (or any persistent factor) and chance, extreme measurements come from combinations of GOOD skill AND GOOD luck. Replicate the measurement, and on average the luck component will be average — so the second measurement regresses toward the underlying skill mean.

Applications:
- Sports: 'sophomore slump' is regression, not psychology.
- Medicine: patients with extreme symptoms tend to improve at the next visit (regression to a less-extreme baseline). Many treatments look effective in uncontrolled trials simply because of regression.
- Education: 'praise reduces performance, criticism improves it' (Kahneman's famous Israeli pilot training observation) — actually regression after extreme performances followed by interventions.
- Finance: top-performing fund managers tend to revert toward average; investors who chase last year's winners underperform.

Correct analysis requires CONTROL groups or careful baseline modelling. Without them, regression masquerades as 'real' effects.
items.why: Performance fluctuations get psychological explanations they don't need. The math of extreme values guarantees that record-breakers tend to come back down. Understanding regression to the mean dissolves many spurious 'effects'.

items.title: P less than 0.05 doesn't mean a result is true — or even probably true
items.claim: A study finds an effect with p = 0.04. Headlines say 'statistically significant'. The reader assumes the effect is real. In fact, in some scientific fields, more than half of 'p < 0.05' findings fail to replicate.

options.text: The probability the effect is real is 96%

The probability of seeing data at least this extreme IF the null hypothesis is true is 4%. Says nothing directly about the probability the effect is real, which requires Bayesian reasoning with priors
The result is wrong 4% of the time
P-values measure the size of effects

items.reveal_title: P-value misinterpretation and the replication crisis
items.reveal:
P-value definition: P(data at least as extreme as observed | null hypothesis true).

Common misinterpretations:
1. P is the probability the null is true (no).
2. (1 - p) is the probability the effect is real (no).
3. P measures effect size (no — small effects in large studies can have tiny p).
4. P < 0.05 means 'real effect' (no — depends on prior plausibility and study design).

Replication crisis (2010s): many influential findings in psychology, biomedicine, economics fail to replicate.
- Open Science Collaboration (2015) attempted to replicate 100 psychology studies. ~36% of replications succeeded (vs ~97% of original studies reporting significance).
- Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology (2021) attempted 23 cancer findings; only 25% of effects were as strong in replication.
- Many famous psychology results (ego depletion, power posing, money priming) have not replicated.

Causes:
- P-hacking (running many tests, reporting only significant ones).
- Publication bias (significant findings published; null results filed away).
- Small samples + multiple testing.
- Garden of forking paths (each analytic choice creates uncounted tests).
- Underpowered studies (true effects mixed with noise; significant results when found are overestimates).

Reforms: preregistration, registered reports, focus on effect sizes and confidence intervals, replication studies, statistical training reform, banishing the 0.05 threshold (some journals).

Bayesian alternatives: P(hypothesis | data) directly. Requires explicit priors but gives more interpretable answers.

The ASA's 2016 statement on p-values: don't use 'p < 0.05' as the sole basis for conclusions. Distance is being made from this old standard.
items.why: P-values look like simple measures of certainty. They aren't. Misinterpreting them has contributed to a massive scientific replication crisis. Understanding what p-values do and don't say is essential to reading research.

items.title: You can estimate pi by dropping a needle on a striped floor
items.claim: A floor has parallel lines spaced apart by distance L. Drop a needle of length L randomly. The probability the needle crosses a line is exactly 2/pi.
items.prompt: Why does pi appear in a problem with no circles?

options.text: The probability calculation involves integrating over the needle's random angle (a continuous variable on [0, pi]) and over its random position (linear), and the integral of sin theta from 0 to pi equals 2 — bringing pi into the denominator
Only works if the floor is circular

items.reveal:
Comte de Buffon set up the problem in 1733. Let d be the perpendicular distance from the needle's centre to the nearest line, and theta the angle the needle makes with the lines. The needle crosses a line if d is less than (L/2) sin theta.

Take d uniform on [0, L/2] and theta uniform on [0, pi/2]. Probability of crossing = (1 / (L/2 * pi/2)) * integral over the crossing region.

Working out: P = (2 / pi). So pi appears because the angle integration covers a full half-period of the sine.

This means you can estimate pi by dropping needles randomly: count crossings out of N drops, multiply by N/(2 * crossings) ≈ pi. Mario Lazzarini reported in 1901 having got pi to six decimals by 3408 throws — almost certainly cherry-picked (six decimals would require billions of throws).

Pi shows up in every probability problem involving a uniform-random angle. The constant of integration smuggles it in.
items.why: Pi is associated with circles. It actually appears in many problems involving angular randomness — anywhere a uniform integration over angles is required.
